title: Trigonometry: Law of Sines for SSA Assessment
description: Checkpoint on applying the Law of Sines to SSA cases and identifying one, two, or no possible triangle solutions.

questions.question: Which given information is an SSA case for △ABC?
options: Sides a and b with the included angle ∠C
questions.explanation: ∠A with opposite side a and another side b gives two sides and a non-included angle.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠A = 28°, a = 7, and b = 10. Which value is closest to sin B?
In △ABC, ∠A = 28°, a = 7, and b = 10. The smaller possible ∠B is about 42.1°. How many triangles are possible?
options: Cannot be decided from this information
questions.explanation: The supplement is 137.9°. Since 28° + 137.9° = 165.9°, both B values are valid, so two triangles are possible.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠A = 70°, a = 12, and b = 8. Which conclusion is correct?
options: No triangle is possible because sin B is greater than 1.
The supplement of B must be used instead of the calculator angle.
questions.explanation: sin B = 8 sin 70° / 12 ≈ 0.6265, so B ≈ 38.8°. Its supplement, 141.2°, is invalid because 70° + 141.2° > 180°.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠A = 25°, a = 5, and b = 14. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.explanation: sin B = 14 sin 25° / 5 ≈ 1.183, which is impossible for a real angle, so no triangle is possible.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠A = 55°, a = 15, and b = 13. What is the smaller possible value of ∠B to the nearest tenth?
In △ABC, ∠A = 55°, a = 15, and b = 13. Why is the supplementary angle not valid?
options: It has a different sine value.
55° plus the supplement is greater than 180°.
Supplements are checked only for right triangles.
questions.explanation: The supplement is about 134.8°, and 55° + 134.8° = 189.8°, which cannot leave a positive third angle.

questions.question: If sin B = 0.6 in an SSA problem, both B = sin⁻¹(0.6) and 180° - sin⁻¹(0.6) should be checked.
questions.explanation: Both angles have the same sine value, so both are possible candidates until the triangle angle sum rejects one.

questions.question: If the given angle and the supplementary candidate add to exactly 180°, the supplementary candidate forms a valid triangle.
questions.explanation: A third angle of 0° is not possible in a triangle, so the two known angles must add to less than 180°.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠A = 36°, a = 9, and b = 12. Find the smaller possible value of ∠B to the nearest tenth of a degree.
questions.explanation: sin B = 12 sin 36° / 9 ≈ 0.7837, so the smaller possible angle is B ≈ 51.6°.

questions.question: In △ABC, ∠A = 36°, a = 9, and b = 12. Find the larger possible value of ∠B to the nearest tenth of a degree.
questions.explanation: The larger possible angle is the supplement of 51.6°, so B ≈ 180° - 51.6° = 128.4°. It is valid because 36° + 128.4° < 180°.

questions.question: A classmate says, “My calculator gave one angle, so there can only be one SSA triangle.” Explain the mistake.
questions.correctAnswer: The calculator gives the principal inverse sine angle, but a supplementary angle has the same sine. In SSA, the supplement must also be checked because it may form a second valid triangle.
questions.explanation: The ambiguity comes from sine having the same value for two angles between 0° and 180°. The second angle is accepted only if it leaves a positive third angle.
